l_spot.speaker: LUCIEN
lines: Wait — what is this in your kit? English print? My friend. My dear friend. In this city that little book is a signed confession with a cover.
Oh no. No no no. A book — in ENGLISH — riding in your pocket across my nice safe floor? That is not literature, that is evidence with page numbers.

b_take.speaker: MME BÉRANGER
lines: Give it here. — Paine. 'These are the times that try men's souls.' My husband had the French of it. I will keep this for after the war, monsieur; paper burns, and so do the men who carry it.
To me, not to him. — Thomas Paine. My husband kept the French edition behind the flour. It stays with me until your war and mine are finished. Paper burns, monsieur. So do carriers.

choices.text: It came from Hempstead with me. Keep it safe, Madame.
I'd rather burn it myself than let it out of my hands.

b_keep.speaker: MME BÉRANGER
lines: Then it has crossed one ocean and it can sit out the rest in a flour tin. You will drink a coffee in this room after the war, monsieur, and I will hand it back with the receipt.
From Texas to my flour tin — it has had a war already. It will be here when you come back for it. Men return for books; I have seen it. It is the medals they leave in drawers.

b_burn_refused.speaker: MME BÉRANGER
lines: No. You will not burn it and you will not keep it; both are sentiments and sentiments leak. The flour tin has kept better secrets than yours. After the war, monsieur. That is the arrangement.
Burn it! And mourn it loudly where Fouchet can hear? No. The tin. After the war you may be sentimental on your own floor.
